anchor_text: ballad-makers cannot be able to express it
summary: Ballad-makers were journalists of the age: they wrote cheap, sensational verse on extraordinary events — murders, prodigies, shipwrecks, wonders — printed as broadsheet ballads and sold at fairs and markets. To say the events surpass what 'ballad-makers cannot be able to express' means the wonder is too great even for the Elizabethan media of popular sensationalism. Autolycus himself is a ballad-seller in Act 4.
detail: The broadside ballad was a staple of popular print culture from roughly 1550 onward — single printed sheets with a woodcut, a topical verse text, and a note of the tune to which it was to be sung. Events like two-headed calves, floods, miraculous survivals, and public executions all generated ballads. The same Autolycus who peddles ballads in the sheep-shearing scene (4.4, 'here's one to a very doleful tune, how a usurer's wife was brought to bed of twenty money-bags') is now standing silent while a story he helped set in motion is narrated around him — a structural irony the scene cultivates. anchor_text: stands by like a weather-bitten conduit of many kings' reigns
summary: The Third Gentleman compares the old Shepherd to a stone water-fountain (conduit) that has been standing outdoors through the reigns of several monarchs — worn down by decades of weather but still upright and present. The simile captures two things at once: the Shepherd's antiquity and endurance, and the odd position he now occupies, standing in a king's court, weeping, with no comprehension of the grandeur around him.

'Weather-bitten' conveys the slow erosion of many years of rain and frost — not broken, but visibly aged. The simile is affectionate and quietly comic: this old man who picked up an abandoned baby in a field, raised it as a daughter, and now finds himself at the center of two kingdoms' reunion is likened to old civic furniture — present through history, worn smooth by time, not quite comprehending why people gather around it. anchor_text: that rare Italian master, Julio Romano, who, had he himself eternity, and could put breath into his work, would beguile nature of her custom
summary: Julio Romano (c. 1499-1546) was a real Italian Renaissance painter and architect, a pupil of Raphael. He is the only real contemporary artist Shakespeare names by name in any play. His reputation for virtuoso realism — for figures so lifelike they seemed almost alive — makes him the plausible sculptor of a statue so perfect it could be mistaken for Hermione. The praise that he would 'beguile nature of her custom' means he would make nature redundant: his art copies life so exactly it competes with the real thing.

In practice he was a painter and architect, not a sculptor, which some editors have noted as an error (either Shakespeare's or his source's). The attribution likely comes from Giorgio Vasari's Le Vite de' Piu Eccellenti Pittori (Lives of the Artists, 1550/1568), which praised Romano extravagantly and was the main route by which Italian Renaissance artists were known in Elizabethan England. The phrase 'beguile nature of her custom' means to steal away nature's usual trade — to make art that replaces the original. The play's whole statue-conceit (is it art or is it life?) is threaded through these lines: Romano is credited with a capacity that Paulina will appear to surpass.

anchor_text: you denied to fight with me this other day, because I was no gentleman born
summary: In Elizabethan law and custom, only those 'born' into the gentry — possessing a coat of arms granted by the College of Heralds — had the legal right to engage in a gentleman's duel or to claim a gentleman's social standing. The Clown is recalling that his social inferior status previously disqualified him from such challenges. Now that his foster-sister has been recognized as a princess, he and his father have apparently been elevated by royal grant to 'gentlemen born.'

A heraldic visitation was a periodic inspection of claims to gentle rank; to be listed was to be officially a gentleman, entitled to bear arms and to participate in duels (which were legally reserved to gentlemen). The Clown's insistence that he has been 'a gentleman born any time these four hours' (TLN 3015) is comic because it mistakes the formality of the grant for the biological and temporal fact of birth: rank is now understood as a legal status, not an innate quality, which is precisely what the play has been exploring through Perdita's arc. The Clown's misuse of 'born' as if a fresh legal document retroactively changes his origin is the joke.

anchor_text: Let boors and franklins say it, I'll swear it
summary: A 'boor' was a peasant or rustic — a man of the lowest agricultural class. A 'franklin' was a free landowner, a prosperous yeoman farmer who held his land outright but was not of gentry rank. The Clown means: let those below gentility merely 'say' a thing without formal commitment; he, now a gentleman, can and will 'swear' it — invoking the oath-taking privilege and obligation of the upper class.

The Clown has in fact recently been a franklin at best — his father is an old shepherd, not gentry. His new self-placement above franklins is therefore comic; he is barely a step removed from the category he disdains. The distinction between 'saying' and 'swearing' carries legal weight: a formal oath (on the Bible, before a witness) was a legal act that could be enforced. The Clown's excitement at getting to swear regardless of the truth is a parody of one of the new responsibilities he has misunderstood as a privilege of rank.

anchor_text: thou art a tall fellow of thy hands
summary: 'Tall' here means brave, valiant, or capable — not physically tall. 'A tall fellow of thy hands' means a man of courage and skill, particularly with weapons: someone good in a fight. detail: The phrase 'tall of hands' (or 'tall of his hands') is a fixed colloquial expression in Shakespeare and his contemporaries meaning dexterous and courageous in combat. The comedy is sharpened by the Clown's simultaneous assertion and retraction: he will swear it, he says, even though 'I know thou art no tall fellow of thy hands and that thou wilt be drunk' (TLN 3041-3042). He has fully grasped that his new status entitles him to swear falsely on a friend's behalf — exactly the old gentry custom of perjury for fellowship that Elizabethan moralists criticized — and is delighted by it.

anchor_text: do not say 'tis superstition, that I kneel
summary: In post-Reformation England, kneeling before images — statues or pictures of holy figures — was branded 'superstition' and 'idolatry' by Protestant reformers; it was one of the central charges against Catholic devotional practice. Perdita's pre-emptive defence ('do not say it is superstition') acknowledges a real cultural anxiety her audience would have felt at once when watching a character kneel before a lifelike stone figure.

The Winter's Tale's statue scene plays precisely at this edge: the crowd watching are kings and courtiers in a room that Paulina calls a 'chapel' (5.3.86), making the space quasi-sacred. When Perdita kneels, Leontes nearly kisses the image, and music 'awakens' the figure, the scene walks the line between reverent art-admiration and the forbidden practice of image-veneration that the Elizabethan church had outlawed. The play stages resurrection through theatre while its characters keep disavowing the magic. This tension between art and idolatry is discussed by Orgel and later scholars as central to the scene.

anchor_text: The fixture of her eye has motion in't, As we are mock'd with art
summary: 'Fixture' means fixed or set position — the stillness of the eye as it holds its sculpted gaze. Leontes notices that even this fixed stare seems to have movement within it; he attributes it to the deceptive power of art ('as we are mock'd with art' = as art deceives us). What he reads as artistic illusion is, of course, real motion in a living face.

anchor_text: this affliction has a taste as sweet As any cordial comfort
summary: A 'cordial' was a medicinal drink made to revive or strengthen the heart ('cor' = heart in Latin) — a restorative used against faintness and shock. anchor_text: what fine chisel Could ever yet cut breath
summary: Leontes poses the scene's central impossibility as a rhetorical question: no sculptor can carve breath. The question takes 'cut' (what a chisel literally does to stone) and turns it against the medium — breath cannot be chiselled. The paradox is the play's thesis: what appears to be sculpture is alive.
detail: The formulation belongs to the rhetorical figure of adynaton — an assertion of impossibility used to amplify wonder. Renaissance theories of art, from Pliny to Vasari, praised painters and sculptors who could make their figures seem to breathe; Giulio Romano's epitaph (quoted in Vasari) claimed exactly that he could deceive nature into thinking his painted figures were alive. Shakespeare plants that precise claim earlier (5.2) and then dramatizes it: Leontes' 'cut breath' question is answered by Hermione's actual exhalation. The chisel is also an implicit foil to Prospero's staff and wand — the magician's instrument versus the craftsman's.

anchor_text: I protest against,--I am assisted By wicked powers
summary: 'Wicked powers' means demonic or diabolical aid — evil spirits. Paulina preemptively denies she is a witch or sorceress. In Elizabethan law and belief, a person who could make a statue move or who 'raised the dead' would be strongly suspected of trafficking with demons, a crime tried under the witchcraft statute. Paulina's disclaimer is legally and theologically pointed, not merely reassuring.
detail: The English Witchcraft Act of 1563 (reinforced 1604) made it a capital offence to use conjuration or witchcraft. Reanimating a corpse or a statue was the kind of feat associated with black magic in contemporary handbooks such as Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584). Paulina frames the miracle in the language of Christian orthodoxy — 'lawful,' 'holy,' 'required you do awake your faith' — to place it in the category of divine wonder rather than diabolism. The scene thus requires the audience to decide whether to read it as magic or miracle, and the play never resolves that ambiguity explicitly.

anchor_text: It is requir'd You do awake your faith
summary: The command to 'awake your faith' echoes the New Testament pattern of miracles that require the onlooker's belief — most pointedly the raising of Lazarus (John 11) and Jesus's 'thy faith hath made thee whole.' Faith is the precondition for witnessing a resurrection. Paulina is staging the recovery of Hermione in unmistakably redemptive terms.
detail: The parallel to the Lazarus story (John 11:38-44) is supported by the wider language of the scene: Paulina says 'I'll fill your grave up' (TLN 3173), 'Dear life redeems you' (3175), and instructs Leontes not to 'shun her / Until you see her die again' (3178). All these phrases echo the Johannine language of the resurrection of the dead and the redemption from death. At the same time, the play carefully avoids making the scene a direct Passion allegory: Hermione is not dead (she has been living in hiding) and Paulina is not Christ. The biblical resonance charges the scene with sacred weight while the narrative remains secular romance.

The echo of John 11 (faith as precondition for witnessing a resurrection) is well-supported by the surrounding language ('I'll fill your grave up', 'Dear life redeems you'), and the careful qualification that Hermione is not dead and Paulina is not Christ prevents over-allegorizing — the gloss stays within what the text will bear.

anchor_text: 'Tis time; descend; be stone no more; approach; Strike all that look upon with marvel
summary: Paulina's incantatory series of short commands — each a grammatically complete imperative — works like a spell: 'descend; be stone no more; approach; Strike all that look upon with marvel; Come; I'll fill your grave up; stir; nay, come away.' The rapid-fire imperatives give the verse the rhythm of a magic charm even while their content is the opposite of dark magic. The rhetorical figure is asyndeton — clauses strung without conjunctions, creating urgency.

anchor_text: If this be magic, let it be an art Lawful as eating
summary: Leontes accepts whatever power has restored Hermione, comparing it to eating — the most ordinary and necessary of acts, and an act the church has never forbidden. The simile deliberately deflates the theological charge that magic is diabolical: if this is magic, let it be as unremarkable and innocent as feeding oneself. The comparison between the miraculous and the daily is the scene's emotional resolution.

anchor_text: should be hooted at Like an old tale
summary: Paulina says that telling the story of Hermione's survival would be 'hooted at like an old tale' — dismissed as a preposterous folk-story. The phrase is the play naming its own genre: the title is The Winter's Tale, Mamillius's unfinished tale was 'of sprites and goblins,' and the play belongs to the old-fashioned romance tradition it simultaneously enacts and ironises.
detail: The self-aware moment is part of Shakespeare's late-romance technique, in which characters comment on the implausibility of the very events they are living through (compare Pericles's Gower figure, and the Second Gentleman's speech in 5.2: 'Such a deal of wonder is broken out... that ballad-makers cannot be able to express it'). The 'old tale' label was common dismissal of naive romance; by giving it to Paulina, Shakespeare acknowledges the play's debt to Greene's Pandosto and to the folktale of the lost and found child, while the visible truth of Hermione standing before the audience overrides the label. The scene asks whether the incredible, when it actually happens, is still an 'old tale.'

anchor_text: You gods, look down, And from your sacred vials pour your graces Upon my daughter's head
summary: Hermione calls on 'the gods' — the plural of polytheistic religion, consistent with the play's Sicilian and Delphic setting — asking them to pour down blessings from their 'sacred vials' as one might pour oil or perfume from a ritual vessel. The image of gods dispensing blessings from vessels descends from classical libation ritual, where wine or oil was poured as an offering and sign of divine favour.
detail: The first words Hermione speaks after sixteen years of silence are a prayer over her daughter, not a greeting to her husband. The priority is deliberate: she speaks as a mother before a wife. The vial image, though it has a New Testament resonance too (Revelation 16:1, 'vials of wrath'), is here aligned with the classical polytheism the play deploys throughout its Sicilian half — the same Apollo and oracle-world of 2.1 and 3.2. The gods here are the Olympian powers; the pouring of grace from a vessel (phiale in Greek, patera in Latin) was a standard libation gesture in classical religion. Hermione's prayer seals the scene's movement from cold idolatry-anxiety to warm blessing.

anchor_text: Knowing by Paulina that the oracle Gave hope thou wast in being,--have preserv'd Myself to see the issue
summary: Hermione explains the logic of her sixteen-year concealment: she knew from the oracle's wording ('the king shall live without an heir if that which is lost be not found,' 3.2) that Perdita might still be alive. She kept herself alive to witness the fulfilment of that conditional prophecy — 'to see the issue.' 'Issue' carries both the meaning of outcome and of offspring. This is the first and only explanation the play gives for Hermione's survival.

anchor_text: I, an old turtle, Will wing me to some wither'd bough, and there My mate, that's never to be found again, Lament till I am lost
summary: 'Turtle' here is a turtledove, not a tortoise — the bird that was the classical and Renaissance emblem of faithful, inconsolable love. The turtledove was proverbially monogamous: if its mate died, it was said to mourn alone on a bare bough for the rest of its life. Paulina compares herself to such a bird: Antigonus, her husband, died years ago (eaten by the bear, 3.3), and she will spend her remaining years in faithful widowhood.

anchor_text: Perform'd in this wide gap of time, since first We were dissever'd
summary: 'Wide gap of time' is the play's retrospective name for the sixteen-year break that Time the Chorus described in Act 4. The final speech turns the reunion into an occasion for storytelling — each person must report the 'part perform'd' in the intervening years — which frames the play's improbable plot as a story that is itself now worth hearing.
